extracted.intended_audience: readers of classical Latin poetry; authors/poets interested in patronage and conduct; students of Horace
extracted.subtask_description: A translation of Horace's Epistles (poetic letters) giving moral reflections and practical advice about living, friendship, and relations with patrons; useful for studying classical epistolary poetry and historical norms for authors seeking favor. Contains anecdotes and prescriptive lines about presenting works and soliciting patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting works to a powerful patron (Epistle XIII guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting volumes to Augustus: 'present these volumes to Augustus sealed up if he shall be in health, if in spirits, finally, if he shall ask for them: do not offend out of zeal to me, and industriously bring an odium upon my books [by being] an agent of violent officiousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, procedural rules for delivering an author's books to a ruler/patron: present only under the right circumstances (when he is well, in good spirits, or asks for them); keep the volumes sealed until the proper moment; avoid officiousness or over-eagerness that will create ill-will toward the work or the author. Do not parade or boast about the labor of delivering the poems ('You must not tell publicly, how you sweated with carrying those verses'); carry the books discreetly (avoid clumsy public displays like 'carry my bundle of books under your arm, as a clown does a lamb'). If solicited with entreaty, do your best, but otherwise avoid creating offense; be careful not to stumble or break instructions. (Epistle XIII: instructions to Vinnius Asina.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Soliciting favors from great men: modesty and cautious behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the friendship of great men is a laudable acquisition, yet their favors are ever to be solicited with modesty and caution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice on how an author or aspiring client should approach powerful people: cultivate usefulness and friendliness but solicit favors with restraint and tact. Examples/advice show two approaches: pay court to the great (Aristippus' pragmatic view: 'I play the buffoon for my own advantage... a horse may carry and a great man feed me') versus proud independence (the cynic who refuses patronage and lives poorly). The practical guideline: if you are poor and want to be of service to your friends, you must pay respects to the great; be adaptable to station, but avoid shameless obsequiousness. Use modesty, caution, and appropriate deference when requesting patronage so as not to offend or appear servile, yet recognize the advantage of strategic compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure yourself by your own standard; avoid losing liberty to excessive ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is a truth, that every one ought to measure himself by his own proper foot and standard.' Do not admire great possessions or honors so much that you sacrifice your liberty or contentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normative guideline about personal/professional conduct that applies to authors and citizens: know your proper station and temperament and avoid pursuing great wealth, honors, or popularity at the cost of freedom or peace of mind. Illustrated by anecdotes (Vulteius Maena: from humble auctioneer to rustic owner ruined by anxieties and losses; the stag/horse allegory: fear of poverty leads to loss of liberty) and exhortations (return to what suits you if the pursued life brings misery). For a writer: do not seek excessive outward applause or material gain if it corrupts your disposition; prefer modest, suitable pursuits and remain consistent with your character. Pursue virtue and inner standards rather than transient fame or riches.
